artiest/bros.text:
Bros was an English pop group, formed in 1986 in Camberley in Surrey. The band consisted of the twin brothers Matt and Luke Goss and their school friend Craig Logan. Matt was given a saxophone by their mother's boyfriend, Luke an electronic drum kit. The group was managed by Tom Watkins, the man who also looked after the Pet Shop Boys.

In 1988 Bros broke through with When Will I Be Famous? and I Owe You Nothing, the group's only number one in the United Kingdom. The debut album Push was released on 28 March 1988. Drop the Boy, I Quit and Cat Among the Pigeons also reached the charts. The press spoke of Brosmania: a horde of teenage girls, the Brosettes, held the group in its grip. In September 1988 the London police closed off part of Oxford Street because so many fans had come to a record signing. In early 1989 Logan left because of illness, after which the brothers carried on as a duo. They released The Time in 1989 and Changing Faces in 1991. In 1992 the band split up. In 2017 the brothers got together one more time for two performances at the O2 Arena.

Bros made smooth, danceable pop music and remains known as an example of a teen phenomenon of the 1980s.
artiest/bros.listen: Listen to When Will I Be Famous? and notice the chorus. Try to hear why it sticks in your head so easily.

artiest/brotherhood-of-breath.text:
Brotherhood of Breath was an English–South African big band, founded in the late 1960s by the South African pianist and composer Chris McGregor. The group was an expansion of his earlier band The Blue Notes. Many of its members were South African exiles in London, such as Louis Moholo, Harry Miller, Mongezi Feza and Dudu Pukwana, sometimes joined by Johnny Dyani. Free jazz musicians from London also played in it, among them Evan Parker, Elton Dean, John Surman, Mike Osborne and Harry Beckett. The line-up changed, depending on who was available.

The album Chris McGregor's Brotherhood of Breath was released in 1971 and includes Mra, which was recorded in 1970. Ogun Records, the label of the bassist Harry Miller, released some of the records. The original orchestra came to an end in the late 1970s after the deaths of Mongezi Feza and Harry Miller. In the early 1980s McGregor founded a second version in France with European musicians, among them Louis Sclavis and François Jeanneau. Later releases included Yes Please, Country Cooking and Travelling Somewhere.

The music resembles a blend of Charles Mingus and the experiments of Sun Ra, but has a sound of its own thanks to its South African influences and its carefully thought-out arrangements. In this way the group joined the freedom of free jazz to the lively, singing melodies of South Africa, in the context of people who had left their country.
artiest/brotherhood-of-breath.listen: Listen to Mra. Notice how the horns play a cheerful, South African melody while the soloists soar above it, free and unpredictable.

artiest/brotzmann-schlippenbach-en-benni.text:
This trio consists of three key figures of European free jazz: the German saxophonist and clarinettist Peter Brötzmann, the German pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach and the Dutch drummer Han Bennink. Brötzmann was born in 1941 in Remscheid, studied painting in Wuppertal and came into contact with Fluxus. A concert by Sidney Bechet made a great impression on him, as did the music of Miles Davis and John Coltrane. He taught himself to play clarinet and saxophone and designed most of his sleeves himself. He died in Wuppertal in 2023.

His album Machine Gun from 1968, an octet recording, was released on his own label and sold at concerts. It is regarded as a milestone of twentieth-century free jazz. He got the nickname Machine Gun from Don Cherry, to describe his violent style of playing. Han Bennink played on Nipples from 1969 and later became his regular partner, and Brötzmann was a member of Bennink's Instant Composers Pool. In 1977 they recorded the duo album Schwarzwaldfahrt together in the Black Forest, with Bennink also hitting trees and other objects. Schlippenbach played on the album Alarm in 1981.

Fifty Years After from 2018 brings the three together again. The trio stands for a jazz in which listening matters more than agreements, and in which energy, humour and sound itself are the subject.
artiest/brotzmann-schlippenbach-en-benni.listen: Listen to Fifty Years After. Notice how the three keep interrupting and following one another, and how Bennink on his drums sometimes plays a joke rather than a rhythm.

artiest/bruce-channel.text:
Bruce Channel is an American singer and songwriter, born in 1940 in Jacksonville, Texas. He came from a musical family and could sing and play guitar at the age of five. While he was still at school, the family moved to Dallas, where he performed at benefit evenings and in youth centres. He then worked briefly for a company that made butane tanks. Later he sang country music on the radio programme Louisiana Hayride, together with the harmonica player Delbert McClinton. He travelled to the studio by train every Saturday for it and made little from each performance.

In 1959 he wrote Hey! Baby with Margaret Cobb. He played the song live for two years before recording it for the producer Bill Smith of Fort Worth. It was first released on Smith's label LeCam, but when it sold well, Smash Records, a subsidiary of Mercury, took over distribution. In March 1962 it reached number one in the United States, for three weeks, and in the United Kingdom it reached number two. It sold more than a million copies and was awarded a gold disc. His album is also called Hey! Baby.

Channel fits somewhere between rock 'n' roll, country and early pop. Hey! Baby is an example of how a simple song with one recognisable instrument could become a worldwide hit, and it belongs to the sound of the early 1960s.
artiest/bruce-channel.listen: Listen to Hey! Baby and notice the harmonica. Notice too how short and simple the melody is and how often it returns.

artiest/bruce-dickinson.text:
Bruce Dickinson is an English heavy metal singer, born in 1958 in Worksop, Nottinghamshire. He grew up in Sheffield, sang in pub bands in the 1970s during his school days and his studies in London, and in 1979 joined Samson, under the stage name Bruce Bruce. In 1981 he left that band to become the singer of Iron Maiden, succeeding Paul Di'Anno. His debut with the group was the album The Number of the Beast in 1982.

During his first period, from 1981 to 1993, Iron Maiden achieved platinum and gold albums in the United States and the United Kingdom in the 1980s and early 1990s. In 1993 he left to go solo, with, among others, Tattooed Millionaire in 1990, Balls to Picasso in 1994 and The Chemical Wedding in 1998. In 1999 he returned to Iron Maiden, together with the guitarist Adrian Smith. Since then the solo albums Tyranny of Souls in 2005 and The Mandrake Project in 2024 have also appeared.

Dickinson is known for his range and his almost operatic style, and for his energetic performances. Outside music he was a professional pilot and flew Iron Maiden's converted charter plane on tour, presented a radio show on BBC Radio 6 Music, wrote novels and took up fencing. His voice became a hallmark of British heavy metal.
artiest/bruce-dickinson.listen: Listen to The Number of the Beast and notice how Dickinson sings: high, powerful and with a long breath, above two heavy guitars.

artiest/bruce-springsteen.text:
Bruce Springsteen was born in 1949 in Long Branch, New Jersey, and grew up in nearby Freehold. He is the face of heartland rock: rock about ordinary people, work, cars and the dream of escaping from a small town. Since 1972 he has played with the E Street Band, and his nickname The Boss dates from those years too.

His debut Greetings from Asbury Park, N.J. was released in January 1973 on Columbia. The breakthrough came with Born to Run (1975). He worked on the title track from January to August 1974, with more than ten layers of guitar, organ, glockenspiel, strings and the saxophone of Clarence Clemons, after the example of the 'wall of sound' of the 1960s. In October 1975 he was on the cover of both Time and Newsweek in the same week. Darkness on the Edge of Town (1978) and The River (1980) followed. He recorded Nebraska (1982) at home as demos, sparse and acoustic. Born in the U.S.A. (1984) yielded seven singles that reached the American top ten.

The title track sounds like an anthem, but is about a Vietnam veteran who is abandoned by his country after coming home. When Ronald Reagan praised him in a campaign speech in 1984, Springsteen rejected it. On 19 July 1988 he played in East Berlin to an enormous crowd and sang Bob Dylan's Chimes of Freedom. With The Rising (2002) he responded to the attacks of 11 September.
artiest/bruce-springsteen.listen: Born in the U.S.A. opens with a synthesizer riff by Roy Bittan on a Yamaha CS-80. Then Max Weinberg's snare drum comes in, with a hard, cut-off reverb (gated reverb). Meanwhile, read along with the lyrics of the verse: the sound celebrates, the words accuse.

artiest/bryan-adams.text:
Bryan Adams is a Canadian singer, songwriter, producer and photographer, born in 1959 in Kingston, Ontario. His father was an officer and later a diplomat, so the family lived in Lisbon, Israel, Japan and South Korea, among other places. Adams grew up in Ottawa and North Vancouver, bought an electric guitar at the age of ten and left school at fifteen. He admired guitarists such as Ritchie Blackmore, Peter Frampton and Steve Marriott.

His debut album was released in 1980, when he was twenty. The breakthrough in North America came with Cuts Like a Knife in 1983 and the ballad Straight from the Heart. Reckless in 1984 made him world famous, with Run to You, Summer of '69 and the power ballad Heaven, which reached number one in the United States. Into the Fire followed in 1987. In 1991 he released (Everything I Do) I Do It for You, which reached number one in at least nineteen countries and spent sixteen weeks in a row at the top in the United Kingdom. It was on Waking Up the Neighbours. From 1993 his hits were mainly ballads, such as Please Forgive Me, All for Love and Have You Ever Really Loved a Woman?.

Adams combines clear rock guitars with a raw, warm voice and melodies that stick in your head at once. He won twenty Juno Awards and a Grammy and also wrote for films. In this way he became one of the best-known Canadian pop artists.
artiest/bryan-adams.listen: Listen to Summer of '69 and notice the guitars and the chorus. Hear how the raw voice rises above a straightforward rock rhythm.

artiest/bryce-dessner.text:
Bryce Dessner is an American composer and guitarist, born in 1976 and living in Paris. He grew up in Cincinnati, Ohio, together with his twin brother Aaron. Together they form the core of the rock band The National, whose music they write in collaboration with the singer and lyricist Matt Berninger. Bryce studied music at Yale University, where he took both his bachelor's and his master's degree.

Besides the band he is an independent composer. His orchestral, chamber and choral works have been commissioned by, among others, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Kronos Quartet, Carnegie Hall and the New York City Ballet. His Murder Ballades is on Filament by the ensemble eighth blackbird, which won a Grammy in 2016. He has worked with Philip Glass, Steve Reich, Paul Simon, Nick Cave, Jonny Greenwood and Taylor Swift. He has composed music for films such as The Revenant, The Two Popes, C'mon C'mon and Cyrano, wrote Music for Wood and Strings with Sō Percussion and founded the MusicNOW Festival. In 2026 he received his first Oscar nomination, for Train Dreams.

His compositions draw their material from the Baroque and folk music, late Romanticism, modernism and minimalism. Dessner shows how a pop guitarist can find a place among classical ensembles and in the film world without letting go of his rock roots.
artiest/bryce-dessner.listen: Listen to Music for Wood and Strings and notice how rhythmic patterns of wood and strings alternate. Try to hear how a repeated motif slowly shifts.

artiest/bts.text:
BTS is a South Korean boy band formed in 2010 by Bang Si-hyuk, the head of Big Hit Entertainment. He first wanted to build a hip-hop group around the rapper RM, but in the end chose an idol group of seven members: Jin, Suga, J-Hope, RM, Jimin, V and Jung Kook. Unlike most K-pop groups, the members were given room to write and produce for themselves as well. In 2013 BTS made its debut with 2 Cool 4 Skool, with a 1990s hip-hop sound and lyrics about the pressure on Korean schoolchildren.

After that the group broadened its style. Dark & Wild (2014), Wings (2016) and the Love Yourself series followed one another quickly, with lyrics about mental health, growing up, self-love and the downside of fame. With Love Yourself: Tear, BTS became the first South Korean act to top the Billboard 200 in 2018. Map of the Soul: 7 was released in 2020, and that same year the English-language Dynamite became the first number 1 by an entirely South Korean act on the Billboard Hot 100. The song also earned a Grammy nomination. After a break for the military service of all the members, the group returned in 2026 with Arirang.

BTS shows how pop crosses borders in the twenty-first century. The fans, who call themselves A.R.M.Y., spread the music through social media and won the group a Billboard award as Top Social Artist in 2017. In this way a Korean group grew into a worldwide act, which even addressed the United Nations.
artiest/bts.listen: Listen to Dynamite and notice the bass line and the horns, which give the song its 1970s disco feel. Hear also how the members' voices keep alternating.

artiest/bubber-miley.text:
James Wesley Miley, known as Bubber, was an American trumpeter and cornettist of early jazz. He was born in 1903 in Aiken, South Carolina, and grew up in New York. He played in small clubs and on boat trips around the city and toured with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds. In Chicago he heard King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band and was impressed by Oliver's use of mutes. Miley found his own voice by combining the straight mute and the plunger with a growling sound.

In 1923 he joined Duke Ellington, who by then was already the de facto leader of the Washingtonians. His solos are on early Ellington tracks such as Black and Tan Fantasy, East St. Louis Toodle-Oo, The Mooche and Creole Love Call. His melodies often borrowed from Baptist hymns from his church. Together with the trombonist Joe Nanton he devised the wah-wah sound that characterises the early Ellington style, the so-called jungle music of the Kentucky Club and the Cotton Club. In 1929 he left the band, mainly because of his drinking problem. After that he still played with Noble Sissle, King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton and Hoagy Carmichael. In 1932 he died of tuberculosis at the age of 29.

Miley shows how a trumpet can talk, cry and growl. His influence lived on in Cootie Williams and later Ray Nance, who took over his style when needed, and in every jazz trumpeter who uses a mute as a voice.
artiest/bubber-miley.listen: Listen to Creole Love Call or East St. Louis Toodle-Oo by Ellington's orchestra. Notice the trumpet with the mute sounding like a voice, growling and wah-wah.

artiest/buck-owens.text:
Alvis Edgar Owens Jr., better known as Buck Owens, was an American singer and songwriter, born in 1929 on a farm in Sherman, Texas. Buck was originally the name of a donkey on the farm. As a boy he announced one day that this was his name too, and it stuck. He later settled in Bakersfield, California, and became the frontman of The Buckaroos.

With that band he reached number one on Billboard's country chart 21 times. His records came out at a rapid pace in the 1960s, among them Buck Owens in 1961, On the Bandstand in 1963, I've Got a Tiger by the Tail in 1965, Open Up Your Heart in 1966 and Your Tender Loving Care in 1967. From 1969 to 1986 he co-hosted the TV show Hee Haw on CBS with Roy Clark. The death of his best friend Don Rich in 1974 left him despondent for years. He did not return until the late 1980s.

Owens was the pioneer of the Bakersfield sound, which he preferred to call American music. The sound of the Buckaroos was bare and direct: simple little stories, catchy choruses, a sharp electric guitar, a solid, driving drum part and high two-part singing by Owens and the guitarist Don Rich. That is far removed from the smooth Nashville productions. Owens is in the Country Music Hall of Fame.
artiest/buck-owens.listen: Listen to I've Got a Tiger by the Tail and notice the sharp, twanging electric guitar and the solid drums. Hear too how the high two-voice singing rides together over the tight accompaniment.

artiest/buckshot-lefonque.text:
Buckshot LeFonque was a musical project led by the saxophonist Branford Marsalis. The name comes from Buckshot La Funke, a pseudonym that Julian Cannonball Adderley used for contractual reasons on the 1958 album Here Comes Louis Smith. Marsalis had played with Sting, Miles Davis and others and wanted to make a new sound by combining classic jazz with rock, pop, R&B and hip-hop.

It began as a collaboration between Marsalis and the DJ and producer DJ Premier. In 1992 Marsalis moved from New York to Los Angeles to become musical director of The Tonight Show, where Jay Leno was the new host. At his house in Los Angeles he received DJ Premier and the sound engineer Ben Austin and began work on the first album. He put together a band from jazz players of The Tonight Show Band, among them Jeff Tain Watts, Robert Hurst, Kenny Kirkland and Kevin Eubanks. Recording took place in Sony Studios in the summer of 1993.

Two albums were released: Buckshot LeFonque in 1994, largely with productions by DJ Premier, and Music Evolution in 1997, on which Frank McComb mainly sings. The trombonist Delfeayo Marsalis and the rapper Uptown also often took part. The project belongs among the attempts of the 1990s to bring jazz and hip-hop together.
artiest/buckshot-lefonque.listen: Listen to a track from the album Buckshot LeFonque. Notice the interplay of hip-hop beats and saxophone, and hear which of the two takes the lead.

artiest/bud-freeman.text:
Lawrence Bud Freeman (1906 to 1991) was an American jazz musician, bandleader and composer, best known as a tenor saxophonist, though he also played clarinet. In 1922 he formed the Austin High School Gang in Chicago with school friends. He first played C-melody saxophone, with band members such as Jimmy McPartland and Frank Teschemacher, and two years later switched to tenor saxophone. The group was influenced by the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Louis Armstrong. Freeman and McPartland went to listen to King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band at the Lincoln Gardens.

In 1927 he moved to New York and worked as a studio musician and band member with, among others, Red Nichols, Ben Pollack and Joe Venuti. His solo on Eddie Condon's 1933 recording The Eel gave him his nickname, after his long, snakelike improvisations. He played in Tommy Dorsey's orchestra from 1936 to 1938 and with Benny Goodman in 1938. After the war he led groups of his own and worked with Buck Clayton, Ruby Braff and Jo Jones. In 1960 he wrote the book and lyrics for the musical Beg, Borrow or Steal, with the ballad Zen Is When. In 1974 he moved to England.

Freeman is one of the first important white tenor saxophonists and brought the Chicago style into the swing era. His searching, flowing tone sounds different from the heavier style of Coleman Hawkins.
artiest/bud-freeman.listen: Listen to The Eel in the version by Eddie Condon and follow the tenor saxophone. Notice how the long phrases keep running on and hardly ever pause.

artiest/bud-isaacs.text:
Forrest Bud Isaacs (1928 to 2016) was an American pedal steel guitarist, born in Bedford, Indiana. His mother enrolled him for lessons at a music shop in town. He began on an ordinary acoustic guitar in Hawaiian style, held horizontally on his knees, but soon preferred the lap steel style and the tunings of Noel Boggs. At fourteen he played with Pee Wee King's band at the Grand Ole Opry. A job was withdrawn when it turned out how young he was. At sixteen he bought a Gibson Electraharp, one of the first steel guitars with pedals, and left school to become a professional musician.

His best-known contribution is his playing on Webb Pierce's Slowly from 1954, a big hit and one of the most played country songs of that year. Isaacs was the first to press a pedal while the strings were still sounding. In this way he could bend a note upwards from below to a tone that was already sounding, something that was not possible on older steel guitars. He played with Red Foley, Little Jimmy Dickens and Chet Atkins, and was for years a member of the house band of the Grand Ole Opry and of the Ozark Jubilee. From 1954 to 1960 he recorded solo for RCA, including Bud's Bounce.

That weeping, gliding sound became a hallmark of country music. In 1984 Isaacs was inducted into the Steel Guitar Hall of Fame.
artiest/bud-isaacs.listen: Listen to Slowly by Webb Pierce and notice the steel guitar. Hear how a note glides up from below and joins another note.

artiest/bud-powell.text: Bud Powell translated the bebop of Charlie Parker to the piano. He grew up in Harlem and admired the technique of Art Tatum. Thelonious Monk took him under his wing as a young pianist at Minton's. With his right hand Powell played long, fast lines like a saxophonist, while the left hand strikes short chords at uneven moments. That way of playing became the model for almost all modern jazz pianists. He wrote pieces such as Un Poco Loco and Tempus Fugue-It. After a brutal beating by the police in 1945 he had mental health problems all his life. From 1959 to 1964 he lived in Paris. He died in New York in 1966.
artiest/bud-powell.listen: Hear the right hand playing like a saxophone, and the short stabs of the left hand.

artiest/bud-shank.text:
Clifford Everett Bud Shank Jr. (1926 to 2009) was an American alto saxophonist and flautist, born in Dayton, Ohio. He began on clarinet, switched to saxophone and in 1946 moved to California, where he played with Charlie Barnet. In 1949 he joined Stan Kenton and broke through as lead alto and flute in Kenton's Innovations in Modern Music Orchestra. In 1951 he left Kenton and worked as a sideman in small jazz groups, including those of Shorty Rogers, Maynard Ferguson and Shelly Manne, and from 1952 with Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse All-Stars. In this way he became one of the faces of jazz on the American West Coast.

In 1953 and 1954 he played Brazilian-tinged jazz with Laurindo Almeida. The album Brazilliance was a great success and brought him awards from DownBeat and Metronome. In the 1960s he was a regular studio musician in Hollywood. Almost everyone knows his flute solo on California Dreamin' by the Mamas & the Papas from 1965. He also made the music for Bruce Brown's surf films with his group and played Harlem Nocturne as the theme music of Mike Hammer. In the 1970s and 1980s he played with the L.A. Four. In the late 1980s he gave up the flute and played only alto saxophone.

Shank shows how jazz, film, pop and world music ran together on the West Coast, with a light, clear tone on alto saxophone and flute.
artiest/bud-shank.listen: Listen to the flute solo in California Dreamin' by the Mamas & the Papas. Notice the soft, woody sound of the alto flute between the vocals.

artiest/buddy-bolden.text:
Charles Joseph Buddy Bolden (1877 to 1931) was an American cornettist from New Orleans. His contemporaries and later jazz historians see him as a key figure in the development of the New Orleans style of ragtime, then called jass, which later came to be called jazz. He lost his father when he was six and grew up with his mother and other relatives. As King Bolden, his band was at the height of its fame in the city from about 1900 to 1907.

Bolden played loudly and improvised a great deal. He did not copy other cornettists, but played by ear what he heard and adapted it for his instrument. In this way he mixed ragtime, church music, march music and blues. He arranged the ordinary New Orleans dance band differently: string instruments became the rhythm section, while at the front played clarinets, trombones and his cornet. His band is said to have been the first in which brass players played blues. One of his best-known songs is Funky Butt, later Buddy Bolden's Blues, one of the earliest references to the idea of funk in popular music. The Big Four, a new syncopated bass drum pattern that loosened up march rhythms, is also attributed to him. Joe King Oliver and Freddie Keppard were directly inspired by him.

In 1907, at the age of thirty, he suffered an acute psychosis and was committed to a psychiatric institution in Jackson, where he remained for the rest of his life. No recordings have survived, but his influence echoes in everything that later came out of New Orleans.
artiest/buddy-bolden.listen: Listen to an old New Orleans performance of Buddy Bolden's Blues and notice how the horns and the rhythm catch each other. Hear how a march rhythm sounds looser and more swinging.

artiest/buddy-holly.text:
Buddy Holly's real name was Charles Hardin Holley, and he was born on 7 September 1936 in Lubbock, Texas. He came from a musical family and learned guitar from his brother Travis. At first he played country music, including in the duo Buddy and Bob with his friend Bob Montgomery. In 1955 he played a few times as the opening act for Elvis Presley, and after that his music became rock 'n' roll.

At the record company Decca he was given little freedom. He therefore went to the producer Norman Petty in Clovis, New Mexico, where he recorded That'll Be the Day with his band The Crickets. In September 1957 that song topped the charts in America and England. A month later came Peggy Sue, and Oh Boy! and Maybe Baby also became well known. On 3 February 1959 he was killed, at only 22 years old, in a plane crash after a concert in Clear Lake, Iowa. Ritchie Valens and The Big Bopper were also killed. Don McLean later called that day, in American Pie, the day the music died.

In his short career Holly wrote and recorded many songs. He is regarded as the musician who established the classic rock line-up: two guitars, bass and drums. His influence on later artists was great, from Bob Dylan, The Beatles and The Rolling Stones to Eric Clapton and Elton John. In 1986 he was among the first artists inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/buddy-holly.listen: Listen to That'll Be the Day (1957). Notice the small line-up of guitars, bass and drums, and the way Holly sometimes lets his voice break off briefly, a hiccup in his singing that became his trademark.

artiest/buddy-rich.text:
Bernard Buddy Rich (1917 to 1987) was an American jazz drummer, songwriter, conductor and bandleader, born in Brooklyn. His parents were vaudeville performers and he became part of their act at the age of eighteen months. At four he was on Broadway as Baby Traps the Drum Wonder, and as a teenager he was one of the best-paid child performers of the 1930s. In 1937 he began to play jazz, with Bunny Berigan, Artie Shaw, Tommy Dorsey, Count Basie and Harry James, among others. In 1942 he joined the Marines. In 1946 he started a band of his own with the support of Frank Sinatra.

In 1956 he made the album Krupa and Rich with Gene Krupa, on which they traded drum solos for six minutes in Bernie's Tune. In 1959 Rich versus Roach followed, with Max Roach. He also played on sessions for Ella Fitzgerald, Louis Armstrong and the Oscar Peterson trio. In 1968 he made Rich à la Rakha with the tabla player Alla Rakha. From 1966 until his death he led the Buddy Rich Big Band, at a time when big bands had gone out of fashion. An arrangement of West Side Story became a fixture of his performances. Rich could not read sheet music and learned his parts by heart.

He was known for technical virtuosity, power and speed and is regarded as one of the most influential drummers of all time. He held that the drummer is the real quarterback of a band.
artiest/buddy-rich.listen: Listen to Bernie's Tune on Krupa and Rich and notice how the two drummers alternate. Try to hear where Rich shows his speed and power.

artiest/buena-vista-social-club.text:
Buena Vista Social Club was a musical ensemble of mainly Cuban musicians, formed in 1996. Nick Gold of the label World Circuit organised the project, the American guitarist Ry Cooder produced it and Juan de Marcos González led it. The name comes from a private club in the Havana district of Buenavista, which was a popular music hall in the 1940s. To bring out the styles of that time, such as son, bolero and danzón, a dozen experienced musicians were brought together, some of whom had not performed for years.

The album Buena Vista Social Club was recorded in March 1996 and released in September 1997. It quickly became an international success, with Chan Chan among its tracks. In 1998 the ensemble performed with a full line-up in Amsterdam and New York. The German director Wim Wenders recorded this in a documentary with interviews from Havana. The film was released in 1999, was nominated for an Oscar and won the award for best documentary at the European Film Awards. In 2017 came Buena Vista Social Club: Adios.

The success brought new interest in traditional Cuban and Latin American music. Some of the musicians went on to make solo albums and worked with stars from other genres. The name became a kind of brand for the golden musical era of Cuba between the 1930s and the 1950s. The best-known members, Compay Segundo, Rubén González and Ibrahim Ferrer, died between 2003 and 2005. Eliades Ochoa, Omara Portuondo and Barbarito Torres are still touring.
artiest/buena-vista-social-club.listen: Listen to Chan Chan. Notice the relaxed tempo, the acoustic guitar and the low, calm singing voice that tells the story without hurry.

artiest/bugge-wesseltoft.text:
Bugge Wesseltoft is a Norwegian jazz pianist, composer and producer, born in 1964, the son of the jazz guitarist Erik Wesseltoft. In 1989 he worked with Knut Riisnæs's quartet and shortly afterwards, at the request of Arild Andersen, he made music for the festival Vossajazz, which appeared on the album Sagn in 1990. He also worked with Jan Garbarek on Molde Canticle, released on I Took Up the Runes from 1990. In this way, in the early 1990s, he influenced the Norwegian jazz scene, which was then moving from the Nordic jazz tradition, known from the label ECM, to what has come to be called future jazz or nu jazz.

He released music on his own label Jazzland and worked with, among others, Terje Rypdal, Jon Eberson, Billy Cobham and the singer Sidsel Endresen. In 1995 he founded the band New Conception of Jazz. Their first album received a Spellemannprisen in 1996. Among later releases were It's Snowing on My Piano in 1997, Sharing in 1998, Moving in 2001 and The Cool Side of the Pillow in 2003. On Sharing he used club DJs and scratchers on a large scale, which surprised many listeners. His track Existence can be heard in the film Extension du domaine de la lutte.

Wesseltoft chose electronic music and does not want to be tied to genre boundaries. He draws hip-hop and other modern dance music into his idea of contemporary jazz. In this way he belongs among the musicians who brought jazz closer to the club in the 1990s.
artiest/bugge-wesseltoft.listen: Listen to a track from New Conception of Jazz or Sharing. Notice the electronic beats and the piano, and hear how a club rhythm and a jazz melody form a single whole.

artiest/bunny-wailer.text:
Bunny Wailer's real name was Neville O'Riley Livingston. He was born in 1947 in Kingston, Jamaica, and spent his earliest years in the village of Nine Mile. There he met Bob Marley. Later his father lived with Marley's mother in Trenchtown, which made the two boys a kind of stepbrothers. In 1963, with their friend Peter Tosh, they began the group that was first called The Wailing Wailers and later The Wailers.

In the early years Bunny sang lead less often than Marley and Tosh, but his voice was indispensable in the group's typical harmony singing. He was influenced by gospel and by the soul singer Curtis Mayfield. When Marley spent a time in the United States in 1966, Bunny himself sang songs such as Who Feels It Knows It. Dreamland became his best-known song. On the album Burnin' he sang Pass It On and Hallelujah Time.

When The Wailers broke through internationally, all the attention fell on Marley. In 1973 Bunny left, also because he had little desire to tour abroad and felt it did not fit his Rastafari convictions. As a solo artist he made roots reggae with political and spiritual lyrics. His 1976 album Blackheart Man is regarded as one of the high points of reggae. He also wrote Electric Boogie for Marcia Griffiths and won three Grammys for best reggae album. He died in 2021.
artiest/bunny-wailer.listen: Listen to a track from Blackheart Man. Notice Bunny Wailer's calm, singing voice above the slow, deep reggae groove, and the spiritual tone of the lyrics.

artiest/burna-boy.text:
Burna Boy, real name Damini Ebunoluwa Ogulu, is a Nigerian singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1991 in Port Harcourt. His mother worked as a translator and later became his manager, and his maternal grandfather was Fela Kuti's manager. He made his first beats with FL Studio and studied for a few years in England. Back in Port Harcourt he did an internship at a radio station. In 2012 he became known with Like to Party, the first single from his debut album L.I.F.E, which came out in 2013.

In 2017 he signed to Atlantic Records. Outside in 2018 was his first album on a major label. African Giant from 2019 won Album of the Year at the All Africa Music Awards and was nominated for a Grammy, and Twice as Tall from 2020 won a Grammy for best world music album. Love, Damini from 2022, which includes Last Last, became the highest-charting Nigerian album on the American Billboard 200. Last Last won two awards at The Headies in 2023. He also became the first African artist with two albums that each have more than a billion streams on Spotify.

His music mixes Afrobeats with reggae, hip-hop and R&B. In this way he brought Nigerian pop music to a worldwide audience, and he is one of the faces of modern Afrobeats.
artiest/burna-boy.listen: Listen to Last Last. Notice the loose, danceable rhythms and how Burna Boy alternates his vocals between singing and half-speaking.

artiest/burt-bacharach.text: Burt Bacharach studied with Darius Milhaud, among others, and worked as an arranger and accompanist for Marlene Dietrich. With the lyricist Hal David he wrote dozens of hits in the 1960s, often for Dionne Warwick. His songs have unusual changes of time signature, surprising chords and a light orchestral sound with flugelhorn, piano and backing vocals. In film he wrote mainly title songs and light scores, such as What's New Pussycat? (1965) and the Bond parody Casino Royale (1967). In it Dusty Springfield sings The Look of Love. For Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) he won two Oscars: for the score and for the song Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head.
artiest/burt-bacharach.listen: Notice the unexpected changes of time signature and chords, and the light arrangements with brass and vocal backing.

artiest/buschi-niebergall.text:
Buschi Niebergall (1938 to 1990) was a German free jazz musician. His first name was Hans-Helmut, and towards the end of his life friends called him Johannes. He was born in Marburg into an academic family: his father was a professor of theology and for a time rector of the university. Niebergall began studying medicine, but stopped when he got to know other musicians as an acoustic guitarist.

As a bassist he was a co-founder of some of the first and most influential free jazz groups in Germany, in the mid-1960s. Examples are Gunter Hampel's Heartplants quintet and Voices, by the quintet of Manfred Schoof, which belong to an independent European development of free jazz. From 1966 he was a member of the Globe Unity Orchestra. He worked with many musicians who improvised freely, among them Peter Brötzmann, Don Cherry, Alfred Harth, Evan Parker, Alexander von Schlippenbach, Irène Schweizer and John Tchicai. In the early 1970s he played in Albert Mangelsdorff's quartets and quintets. Releases under his own name include Open in 1979 and Ballade an der Ruhr in 1980.

After 1980 he chose a withdrawn life in Frankfurt, apart from the occasional project involving jazz and poetry. Niebergall shows that German jazz in the 1960s found a free sound of its own that did not copy what came from America.
artiest/buschi-niebergall.listen: Listen to a recording of the Globe Unity Orchestra and try to follow the double bass. Notice how, in a group of free improvisers, it does not merely accompany but also speaks up.

artiest/butch-vig.text:
Butch Vig, really Bryan David Vig, is an American producer, drummer and songwriter. He was born in 1955 in Viroqua, Wisconsin. As a child he had piano lessons, but after seeing The Who on television he traded the piano for a drum kit. He studied film at the University of Wisconsin and played in local bands such as Spooner and Fire Town. In 1984 he founded the recording studio Smart Studios in Madison with Steve Marker.

In 1991 he broke through as a producer with Gish by The Smashing Pumpkins and above all Nevermind by Nirvana. Where the previous Nirvana album, Bleach, had sounded raw and lo-fi, Vig had the vocals and guitars double-tracked. Kurt Cobain did not want that at first, but Vig convinced him by saying that John Lennon did it too. In this way Nevermind got a full, powerful sound. He then produced Siamese Dream by The Smashing Pumpkins, Dirty by Sonic Youth and later 21st Century Breakdown by Green Day and Wasting Light by the Foo Fighters.

After Nevermind, Vig by his own account had had enough of bands that played only guitar, bass and drums. He therefore started the band Garbage with the Scottish singer Shirley Manson, in which he drums and co-produces. Garbage mixed rock with samples and electronics and scored with Stupid Girl and Only Happy When It Rains. In this way Vig determined to a large extent how alternative rock sounded in the 1990s.
artiest/butch-vig.listen: Listen to Smells Like Teen Spirit by Nirvana, from Nevermind. Notice the difference between the soft verses and the hard chorus, and how full and tight the guitars and drums sound.

artiest/byron-g-harlan.text:
Byron George Harlan (1861 to 1936) was an American singer from Kansas. He was a comic minstrel singer and ballad singer who became best known for his recordings with Arthur Collins. Together they were often credited on records as Collins & Harlan.

Harlan recorded in the early period of the gramophone, when music was captured on cylinders and early discs. His solo recordings ran from 1899 to 1921 and appeared on Edison, Victor, Columbia and Pathé, among others. He sang sentimental ballads such as The Vacant Chair, Always in the Way and With the Robins I'll Return, but also light songs such as School Days and My Gal Sal. With Collins he recorded, among others, They Were All Doing the Same in 1902, and in 1905 In My Merry Oldsmobile, one of the first car songs.

The style belongs to the popular music for the audience of around 1900: clearly articulated singing, simple accompaniment and lyrics with humour or feeling. Harlan belongs among the singers who made up the first record market, even before jazz, blues and rock 'n' roll made their entrance. His work lets us hear what the ordinary listener in America heard at the beginning of the twentieth century.
artiest/byron-g-harlan.listen: Listen to a recording by Collins & Harlan, such as In My Merry Oldsmobile. Notice the clear, measured singing and the limited sound of the old recording technology.

artiest/bzn.text:
BZN, in full Band Zonder Naam (Band Without a Name), was a Dutch pop group from Volendam that existed from 1966 to 2007. The group began as a pop band with harmony singing in the manner of the early Bee Gees. The first line-up consisted of Jan Veerman (vocals), Cees Tol and Evert Woestenburg (guitar), Jan Tuijp (bass guitar) and Gerrit Woestenburg (drums). In the early 1970s the band switched to hard rock and had its first successes. When the singer Veerman left and the drummer Jan Keizer took his place, the group chose commercial middle-of-the-road pop and a female singer joined, Anny Schilder. In this way BZN laid the foundation for its status as the most popular Dutch band in terms of hits and albums.

The big breakthrough came with Mon Amour in 1976, which spent more than five weeks at number one. BZN had 55 hits in the Dutch charts and was the only act with a top 40 hit in 26 consecutive years, from 1973 to 1998. The album Pictures of Moments from 1982 went gold and was the first album by a Dutch group to do so at Phonogram Holland. The band was also successful in South Africa, for example with Yeppa in 1990. In 1984 Carola Smit succeeded Schilder, and in 1988 the brothers Cees and Thomas Tol, who had written most of the music and lyrics, left. In 2003 the group switched to Dutch lyrics. BZN also discovered the young Jan Smit.

In 2005 four members received a royal decoration, and in 2006 and 2007 a farewell tour followed. BZN stands for the smooth, melodic Dutch pop music that many listeners heard almost daily.
artiest/bzn.listen: Listen to Mon Amour and notice the interplay of male and female voice. Hear how soft accompaniment and a clear melody carry the song.

artiest/cab-calloway.text: The singer and bandleader Cab Calloway took Duke Ellington's place at the Cotton Club in 1931. That same year he recorded Minnie the Moocher, with the refrain 'Hi-de-hi-de-ho', which the audience was meant to sing back. He was an exuberant entertainer in a white tailcoat with a big voice, and appeared in films such as Stormy Weather. He even published a dictionary of jive talk. His orchestra was also musically strong: the tenor saxophonist Chu Berry and the young Dizzy Gillespie played in it. Gillespie was fired in 1941 after a quarrel. Calloway kept performing into old age and appeared in the 1980 film The Blues Brothers.
artiest/cab-calloway.listen: Sing along with the call-and-response between singer and band.

artiest/cabaret-voltaire.text:
Cabaret Voltaire is an English group from Sheffield, founded in 1973 by Stephen Mallinder, Richard H. Kirk and Chris Watson. The name comes from the Zürich café where the Dada movement began in the early twentieth century. Watson, a telephone engineer by trade, experimented with electronics to make music without musical instruments. He was inspired by Brian Eno and, together with Kirk, built tape loops and sound collages. Kirk added clarinet and guitar. At the end of 1973 Mallinder joined on vocals and bass guitar.

The early music consisted of home-made electronics, tape recorders and performance in the spirit of Dada, and helped to shape the industrial music of the mid-1970s. The band found its audience in the post-punk era, when they often performed together with Joy Division. That sound can be heard on albums such as Mix-Up in 1979, The Voice of America in 1980 and Red Mecca in 1981. After Watson left in 1981, Mallinder and Kirk carried on as a duo until 1994. They gradually adopted elements of synth-pop, techno, house and funk, including on Micro-Phonies in 1984, Code in 1987 and Plasticity in 1992. From 2009 until his death in 2021 Kirk gave the name new life as a solo project.

Cabaret Voltaire is regarded as one of the most innovative and influential electronic groups of its time. They showed that a synthesizer and a tape recorder can also be a band.
artiest/cabaret-voltaire.listen: Listen to a track from Red Mecca or Micro-Phonies. Notice the electronic sounds and the rhythm, and hear how distorted voice and raw synthesizers create a cold, menacing atmosphere.

artiest/caleb-followill.text:
Caleb Followill is the singer of Kings of Leon, an American rock band formed in 1999 in Mount Juliet, Tennessee. The group consists of the brothers Caleb, Nathan and Jared Followill and their cousin Matthew Followill. The brothers grew up in Oklahoma and Tennessee, where their father Ivan Leon Followill was a minister in the United Pentecostal Church. He preached in churches and at tent meetings in Oklahoma and the Deep South, and the boys travelled with him.

The band's early music mixed Southern rock and garage rock with influences from the blues. Later it developed towards a more alternative rock sound. In the United Kingdom success came first, with nine top 40 singles and two BRIT Awards in 2008. The third album, Because of the Times, reached number one there. After Only by the Night in 2008 the breakthrough in the United States followed too, with the singles Sex on Fire, Use Somebody and Notion. After that came Come Around Sundown in 2010, Mechanical Bull in 2013, Walls in 2016, When You See Yourself in 2021 and Can We Please Have Fun in 2024. For Use Somebody the band received a Grammy for Record of the Year in 2010.

Caleb Followill carries the band with his hoarse, raw voice, which does not hide its roots in church and Southern rock.
artiest/caleb-followill.listen: Listen to Use Somebody and notice Caleb Followill's voice. Hear how the raw vocals build to the chorus, above guitars that keep growing bigger.

artiest/camaron-de-la-isla.text: Camarón de la Isla, born José Monje Cruz into a gitano family in San Fernando near Cádiz, made nine albums with Paco de Lucía between 1969 and 1977. With La leyenda del tiempo (1979) he broke with tradition: electric bass, rock influences and lyrics by Federico García Lorca. Purists were angry, but the album became a foundation for nuevo flamenco. An estimated 100,000 people came to his funeral.
artiest/camaron-de-la-isla.listen: Listen to La Leyenda del Tiempo and hear how his hoarse flamenco voice sounds above an electric bass and drums.

artiest/cameron-graves.text: Cameron Graves is an American pianist and composer from Los Angeles. Two albums have so far been released under his own name: Planetary Prince in 2017 and Seven in 2021. He belongs to the city's new generation of jazz musicians, in which jazz is once again played on a grand and ambitious scale, with the piano as the leading voice.
artiest/cameron-graves.listen: Listen to a track from Planetary Prince and follow the piano. Notice how the band goes along with the movements of the piece.

artiest/camille-saint-saens.text: Camille Saint-Saëns was already 73 and a celebrated composer when in 1908 he wrote music for L'assassinat du duc de Guise, a film by the Paris company Film d'Art. It is one of the first scores composed specially for a single film. Until then, cinema musicians had mainly played existing pieces. Saint-Saëns wrote for a small ensemble with strings, piano and harmonium. He followed the film closely: after an introduction each tableau received a section of its own, with musical reactions to what was happening. Later he gave the work an opus number, Op. 128, so that it also exists as a concert piece. His concert music, such as Danse macabre and Le carnaval des animaux, is still used in films today.
artiest/camille-saint-saens.listen: Notice how short motifs react to the action: tension in the strings, sudden accents at the murder and a solemn ending.

artiest/can.text:
Can was a German experimental rock band formed in Cologne in 1968 by Holger Czukay on bass and tape editing, Irmin Schmidt on keyboards, Michael Karoli on guitar and Jaki Liebezeit on drums. Czukay and Schmidt came from the academic music world and were pupils of Karlheinz Stockhausen. The group was at first called Inner Space and took the name Can at the suggestion of the singer Malcolm Mooney, because of its meaning in various languages. Mooney sang from 1968 to 1970, followed by the Japanese Damo Suzuki until 1973.

They set up a studio of their own in the castle Schloss Nörvenich, where their 1969 debut Monster Movie came into being. Tago Mago followed in 1971, Ege Bamyasi in 1972, which includes Vitamin C, and Future Days in 1973. The singles Spoon in 1971 and I Want More in 1976 reached national charts.

Can mixed psychedelic rock, funk, samba and musique concrète. The music often arose from long improvisations, which were edited afterwards, with a tight, hypnotic drum part by Liebezeit as its foundation. The group is regarded as one of the pioneers of krautrock and has influenced rock, post-punk, indie rock, post-rock and ambient.
artiest/can.listen: Listen to Vitamin C from Ege Bamyasi. Notice Liebezeit's tight, repeating drums and how the bass and guitar build a groove around them without ever hurrying.

artiest/candy-dulfer.text: Candy Dulfer, daughter of the saxophonist Hans Dulfer, began playing saxophone at the age of six, encouraged by her father. As a teenager she already had a band of her own, Funky Stuff, and she played as the opening act for Madonna. Prince asked her to play with him in 1988. In 1989 she recorded Lily Was Here with Dave Stewart of Eurythmics, for the Dutch film of the same name; the single became an international hit. Her album Saxuality (1990) was nominated for a Grammy in the United States. She plays a mixture of funk, pop and smooth jazz and has toured with, among others, Prince, Van Morrison and Pink Floyd.
artiest/candy-dulfer.listen: Hear how the alto saxophone plays funky and direct above a pop beat.

artiest/canned-heat.text:
Canned Heat is an American blues rock band, formed in Los Angeles in 1965. The group arose in the circle of blues collectors around Bob Hite, who had been trading blues records since his youth. At his home in Topanga Canyon he and Alan Wilson, a bottleneck guitarist, first rehearsed as a jug band. The name comes from Tommy Johnson's Canned Heat Blues of 1928, a song about an alcoholic who in desperation began drinking Sterno, known in popular speech as canned heat. The band wanted to increase interest in the blues and in the original blues musicians.

After performances at the Monterey and Woodstock festivals at the end of the 1960s, Canned Heat became world famous. The line-up then consisted of Hite on vocals, Wilson on guitar, harmonica and vocals, Henry Vestine and later Harvey Mandel on lead guitar, Larry Taylor on bass and Adolfo de la Parra on drums. Three songs became international hits: Going Up the Country, On the Road Again and Let's Work Together. Albums such as Boogie With Canned Heat in 1968, Living the Blues in 1968 and Hooker 'n Heat in 1971 show the foundation. In 1970 Wilson died unexpectedly and the line-up often changed after that. De la Parra is one of the few from the 1960s who stayed for a long time.

The band played blues standards and its own work, sometimes with long psychedelic solos, and became one of the popular acts of the hippie era. Canned Heat introduced a young audience to old blues.
artiest/canned-heat.listen: Listen to Going Up the Country and notice the thin-sounding flute and the driving boogie rhythm. Hear how an old blues feeling suddenly sounds cheerful and airy here.

artiest/cannonball-adderley.text: Julian 'Cannonball' Adderley was a music teacher in Florida when in 1955 he sat in at a club in New York and stood out at once. His alto saxophone sounded like Charlie Parker's, but warmer and with more blues and gospel. From 1957 to 1959 he played in Miles Davis's sextet, including on Kind of Blue. After that he led a quintet that played soul jazz, together with his brother, the cornettist Nat Adderley. With This Here (1959) and Mercy, Mercy, Mercy (1966), written by his pianist Joe Zawinul, he had hits. During concerts Adderley addressed the audience and explained the music. He died of a stroke in 1975.
artiest/cannonball-adderley.listen: Notice the audience's reaction: this is jazz where you are allowed to clap along.

artiest/cappella-mediterranea.text:
Cappella Mediterranea is a Baroque ensemble, founded in 2005 by the Argentine conductor Leonardo García Alarcón, born in 1976 in La Plata. García Alarcón studied harpsichord and organ, was for years an assistant to Gabriel Garrido and teaches at the conservatoire in Geneva. The ensemble aims at the aesthetic ideals of composers from Southern Europe in the seventeenth century and also wants to bring music from the folk traditions around the Mediterranean to a wide audience. It specialises in the main genres of that time: the madrigal, the polyphonic motet and opera. It often works with the Chœur de Chambre de Namur, of which García Alarcón has been artistic director since 2010.

The ensemble brings back forgotten music, such as Il Diluvio Universale and Nabucco by the seventeenth-century Sicilian Michelangelo Falvetti, and makes new performances of well-known works such as the Vespers and L'Orfeo by Monteverdi. The international breakthrough came in 2013 with the opera Elena by Francesco Cavalli at the Festival d'Aix-en-Provence. After that it played in major opera houses and at festivals. Albums on the list include Virtuosissima compositrice in 2009, Heroines of the Venetian Baroque in 2015, L'Orfeo in 2021 and La finta pazza in 2022.

In this way Cappella Mediterranea contributes to the rediscovery of Baroque music, a world in which singing, basso continuo and dramatic expression supply the blueprint for much later music.
artiest/cappella-mediterranea.listen: Listen to Monteverdi's L'Orfeo in this ensemble's performance. Notice how the singers sing the text almost as speech and how the accompaniment supports the drama.

artiest/cappella-mediterranea-en-leonard.text:
Cappella Mediterranea is an ensemble for Baroque music, founded by the Argentine conductor Leonardo García Alarcón. He was born in 1976 in La Plata and studied harpsichord and organ. For years he was an assistant to Gabriel Garrido before starting his own ensemble. With Cappella Mediterranea he has performed at many festivals, above all the Festival d'Ambronay. After a performance of Il diluvio universale by Michelangelo Falvetti, a seventeenth-century composer, he was made an honorary citizen of Ambronay.

García Alarcón teaches at the conservatoire in Geneva and researches the way the basso continuo, the fixed accompaniment of bass and chords, was played in the seventeenth century. Together with the violinist Stéphanie de Failly he leads the Ensemble Clematis, and since 2010 he has been artistic director of the Chœur de chambre de Namur and of La Nouvelle Ménestrandie.

The ensemble plays early music in a historically informed way, with attention to rhetoric and colour. In the performance of a madrigal such as Il bianco e dolce cigno by Jacques Arcadelt from 1539, the Renaissance sounds, the time in which poet and composer sought one voice together. In this way the ensemble represents a side of music history that precedes pop music, and yet shows how long people have been singing songs about love.
artiest/cappella-mediterranea-en-leonard.listen: Listen to Il bianco e dolce cigno. Notice how the four or five voices follow one another in calm lines and how the music bends along with the words of the poem.

artiest/cappella-romana.text:
Cappella Romana is a vocal ensemble, founded in 1991 in Portland, Oregon. The name means Roman chapel and refers to the medieval Greek idea of the Roman oikoumene, the inhabited world, to which Rome and Western Europe belonged, but also the Byzantine Empire with Constantinople as the New Rome. The ensemble is best known for its research into Eastern Orthodox chant and contributed to exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. It is directed by Alexander Lingas, a musicologist at City University in London.

In 2010 the ensemble joined the research project Icons of Sound on the acoustics of the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, together with Stanford University. For the album Lost Voices of Hagia Sophia from 2019, digital sound techniques were used to recreate the enormous space, so that Byzantine chants sound as they could be heard a thousand years ago. Other albums are When Augustus Reigned in 2000, The Fall of Constantinople in 2006, Voices of Byzantium in 2012, Cyprus: Between Greek East and Latin West in 2017 and The Akáthistos Hymn in 2018.

The music consists of monophonic and polyphonic choral chants, often over a drone (bourdon), without instruments. Cappella Romana shows how space and singing belong together, and makes an ecclesiastical tradition of more than a thousand years audible to a wide audience.
artiest/cappella-romana.listen: Listen to a chant from Lost Voices of Hagia Sophia. Notice the long reverberation of the space and how the voices rest on a sustained note.
